n: This grand, difficult processional hymn opens with the words Moses spoke whenever the ark set out in the wilderness: let God rise up and scatter his enemies.

f.w: Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered

n: The wicked vanish before God like smoke in the wind or wax near a flame.

f.w: as wax melteth before the fire

n: But the righteous rejoice in God’s presence with great gladness.
Sing to the one who rides across the skies — whose name is JAH, a short form of Jehovah.

f.g: A short form of YHWH (Jehovah), as in “Hallelu-jah” — “praise Jah.”
Hebrew may read “rides through the deserts” or “rides on the clouds.”

n: Mighty as he is, God cares most tenderly for the vulnerable: he is a father to orphans and defender of widows.

f.g: Defender, champion.

n: God gives the lonely a family and frees prisoners, but rebels end up in a barren land.

f.w: God setteth the solitary in families
f.g: Gives the lonely a home.

f.w: he bringeth out those which are bound

n: The psalm recalls God marching ahead of Israel through the wilderness.

f.w: when thou wentest forth before thy people

n: At his coming the earth quaked and the sky poured rain; Sinai itself shook.
God sent abundant rain to refresh his weary land and people.

f.g: Israel’s land, or the people themselves.

n: His people settled in the land, and in his goodness God provided for the poor.

f.g: Possibly “your flock” or “your creatures.”

n: God gave the command, and a great host of women proclaimed the good news of victory. The Hebrew word for “those that published it” is feminine.

f.w: great was the company of those that published it
f.g: The proclaimers are women — like Miriam and the women who celebrated victories.

n: Enemy kings fled in haste, and women at home divided the loot.

f.g: Quickly.
Plunder from the battle.

n: A notoriously hard verse. It seems to say that even those who stayed among the sheepfolds will share in rich treasure, pictured as a dove with silver and gold wings.

f.g: Lain among the sheepfolds or hearth-stones — the Hebrew is uncertain.

f.w: wings of a dove covered with silver
f.g: Possibly a prized trophy, or Israel pictured as a dove.

n: When God scattered the kings, it was like snow falling on Mount Zalmon — perhaps bleached bones, or the glint of scattered weapons.

f.g: Zalmon, a hill near Shechem.

n: Mount Bashan, the majestic many-peaked range to the northeast, is described as a mountain of God.

f.g: A fertile, high region east of the Sea of Galilee; Mount Hermon’s range.

n: The great mountains look on in jealousy, because God chose little Mount Zion as his home forever. God’s choice, not size, makes a place holy.

f.g: Why look with envy?

f.w: the LORD will dwell in it for ever

n: God’s heavenly chariots number in the countless thousands; the Lord comes from Sinai into his sanctuary.

f.w: The chariots of God are twenty thousand

n: God ascends Zion like a victorious king leading captives and receiving tribute. Paul applied this verse to Christ, who ascended to heaven and gave gifts to his Church.

f.w: Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive

f.g: Received tribute among people; Ephesians reads “gave gifts unto men.”

n: Blessed is the Lord who carries our burdens every day — or loads us with blessings. Either way, he is our salvation.

f.g: May also be read “daily bears our burden.”

n: Our God is a God who saves, and escape from death belongs to him alone.

f.g: The ways of escape from death.

n: God will crush the heads of enemies who keep walking in their sins.

f.g: Long hair may signal a warrior’s vow or pride.

n: God says he will bring his enemies back from wherever they flee — from the mountains of Bashan or the depths of the sea — to face justice.

f.w: I will bring again from Bashan

n: Ancient battlefield language for total victory over evil.
Now a procession appears: everyone watches God, the King, march into the sanctuary.

f.g: Processions.

n: Singers lead, musicians follow, and young women play tambourines in the middle.

f.g: Hand drums or tambourines.

n: Bless God in the great assemblies, you who descend from Israel’s fountain — Jacob.

f.g: The source of Israel — Jacob, the ancestor of the tribes.

n: The tribes march in: little Benjamin first (Israel’s first king, Saul, came from it), then Judah’s leaders, and northern tribes Zebulun and Naphtali.

f.g: The smallest tribe, descended from Jacob’s youngest son.

n: Your God has ordained your strength; show your power again, O God, as you have before.
Because of the temple in Jerusalem, foreign kings will bring gifts to God.

f.w: shall kings bring presents unto thee

n: God is asked to rebuke the “beast of the reeds” (perhaps Egypt) and the herds of bull-like nations until they bring silver in tribute. Scatter those who love war.

f.g: Literally “the beast of the reeds” — possibly the crocodile or hippopotamus, a symbol of Egypt.

f.w: scatter thou the people that delight in war

n: Envoys will come from Egypt, and Ethiopia will reach out its hands to God — a vision of distant nations turning to the Lord.

f.w: Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God

f.g: Hebrew Cush — the land south of Egypt.

n: All kingdoms of the earth are invited to sing to the Lord.
He rides across the ancient heavens and thunders with a mighty voice.

f.w: he doth send out his voice

n: Acknowledge God’s power: his majesty is over Israel and his strength is in the skies.

f.g: Give credit, acknowledge.

n: God is awesome from his sanctuary, and he gives strength to his people. The psalm closes simply: “Blessed be God.”

f.w: giveth strength and power unto his people
